title: Indian American Geneticist Pradeep Natarajan to Receive AHA's 2026 Population Research Prize
excerpt: The Harvard and Mass General physician-scientist, who joined Amgen in August to lead human genetics, will be honored on Nov. 8 in Chicago for transforming how genetics and big population studies prevent heart disease.
body:
• Dr. Pradeep Natarajan, an Indian American cardiovascular geneticist, will receive the American Heart Association's 2026 Population Research Prize during the Presidential Session on Sunday, Nov. 8, at the AHA's Scientific Sessions in Chicago (Nov. 6–9, 2026).
  • In August 2026 he joined Amgen as vice president of global research, head of human genetics and head of the Cardiometabolic Therapeutic Area — while continuing as a professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School and a distinguished physician at Massachusetts General Hospital.
  • His research has uncovered genetic mechanisms behind lipid disorders, coronary artery disease, and clonal hematopoiesis, advanced polygenic risk scores for earlier heart-disease detection, and opened new drug targets; he has authored more than 330 peer-reviewed publications and led a $11.2 million NIH Common Fund project.
  • Reader utility: his polygenic risk tools aim to flag elevated cardiovascular risk earlier in life — research with particular resonance for South Asians, who face disproportionately high rates of heart disease.

The scientist behind the prize

Pradeep Natarajan, M.D., M.M.Sc., FAHA, will be honored by the American Heart Association at its annual Scientific Sessions this November, the AHA announced on Sept. 28. The Population Research Prize recognizes his career using human genetics and data from large, diverse populations to transform the understanding and prevention of cardiovascular disease.

Dr. Natarajan's most influential contributions, the AHA said, include advancing the interpretation of whole-genome sequencing for cardiovascular disease, identifying novel genetic pathways in lipid metabolism and coronary artery disease, and developing polygenic risk prediction tools designed to improve prevention. His work integrates genomics, multi-omics, electronic health records, and large population biobanks — spanning international collaborations involving millions of participants — to turn genetic discoveries into clinical care.

"His innovative research has helped bridge genomic discovery with clinical application, advancing precision medicine while improving our understanding of cardiovascular risk across diverse populations."

— Manesh R. Patel, AHA 2026–27 volunteer president

From Berkeley to the top of the field

Natarajan earned his bachelor's degree from the University of California, Berkeley, his medical degree from the University of California, San Francisco, and a master of medical sciences degree in biomedical informatics from Harvard Medical School. He completed his internal medicine residency at Brigham and Women's Hospital, and his cardiovascular medicine fellowship and postdoctoral training in human genetics at Massachusetts General Hospital — all in Boston.

He has been a longtime volunteer leader with the Heart Association since 2011, chairing its Data Science and Precision Medicine Committee since 2024 and serving on the Scientific Sessions Planning Committee since 2021. His honors include election to the American Society for Clinical Investigation in 2022 and the Association of American Physicians in 2024, the AHA's Joseph A. Vita Award in 2023, and the Genomic and Precision Medicine Mid-Career Award in 2025.

"I have dedicated my career to discovering and understanding the drivers of cardiovascular disease using human genetics, innovative methods and interdisciplinary collaboration towards optimal cardiovascular prevention and health."

— Dr. Pradeep Natarajan

The diaspora connection

South Asians in the United States carry some of the highest cardiovascular risk of any ethnic group — a burden rooted in genetics, metabolism, and lifestyle that researchers are still untangling. Natarajan's work on polygenic risk scores, which combine thousands of genetic variants to estimate an individual's heart-disease risk years before symptoms appear, is aimed squarely at this kind of early prevention. His prize is also a marker of how thoroughly Indian Americans have shaped modern medicine's research establishment: physician-scientists of Indian origin now lead some of the country's most consequential genomics programs.

What's next

The Population Research Prize will be presented during the Presidential Session on Sunday, Nov. 8, at the AHA's Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago — a meeting the association calls a premier global exchange of cardiovascular science. Meanwhile, Natarajan's dual perch in industry and academia — leading human genetics at Amgen while teaching at Harvard and seeing patients at Mass General — positions him to push his genetic discoveries toward actual therapies. For the diaspora, it's one more name to watch in the science that could one day protect their own hearts.
